I resort to devotion to the Blessed One, whose crest is a flashing jewel of consciousness,
the moonlight in the courtyard of the mind, a stream through the garden of bliss.
I bow to that <s>Vaiṣṇavī</s> existence, pervading the three worlds with blossoming, shining, exultant power,

children.text: yā pūrvakoṭirbhāvānāṃ sattāṃ tāṃ vaiṣṇavīṃ namaḥ ||
children.translated_text: which is the primal limit of beings.
For creatures, like waters hanging at the edge of a lotus-grove shaken by wind,
<s>Hari</s> alone is remembered as stability.
Homage to him whose self is the sun, who possesses rays of consciousness,
who causes the beauty of the heart-lotus bud to open.
Homage to him whom sages, having passed beyond death, behold

children.text: paramaṃ puruṣaṃ pāre tamasāṃ mahasāṃ tathā ||
children.translated_text: as the supreme <s>Puruṣa</s>, beyond darkness and also beyond radiance.
Homage to him as sacrifice, as the oblation of sacrifice, and as the self made of sacrificial soma
Salutation to him who is the swan, the vehicle of <s>Sarasvatī</s>, who has every form.
To truth, to the treasury of <s>dharma</s> (sacred order), to the knower of the field, to the immortal self,
to the foundation of <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and <s>Yoga</s>, salutation to the sole cause of liberation.
Salutation to the terrible one, the treasury of illusion, the thousand-headed one,
to him whose nature is yogic sleep, from whose navel-lotus the creator of the world arose.
Salutation to him whose form is water, who is the cause in the world's continuance,
to dire Time, to the mighty one, to life, whose nature is wind.
To Time, to the abode of the classes and colors, whose self consists of all worlds,
to the breath of the worlds, to the being of all creatures, salutation to the universal creator.
To the fulfilled one, with the body of a lion, the destroyer of demons,
to valor, to endless greatness, salutation to the bearer of the world's burden.
To the maker of worldly existence, to delusion, to knowledge that cuts through darkness,
to the inconceivable abode, the hidden one, to <s>Rudra</s>, the matted-haired one, salutation.
To the peaceful one, lying in the state of isolation whose waves are stilled,
to him who transcends every condition, whose self is made of all things, salutation.
Dark as a grove of blue lotuses, with the shimmer of quivering filaments,
wearing his two garments, I praise <s>Viṣṇu</s>, a tonic for the eyes.
Having spoken thus, filled with abundant bliss, and bowing in his mind to <s>Hari</s>,
the son of <s>Śāntanu</s> meditated, with tears, while he was praised by the great seers.
Then, together with the sons of <s>Pāṇḍu</s>, in chariots of deep sound,
<s>Keśava</s>, the friend of <s>Sātyaki</s>, came with <s>Saṃjaya</s> and the others.
<s>Kṛṣṇa</s> came to <s>Kurukṣetra</s>; seeing those lakes of <s>Bhārgava</s>,
he told <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s> the righteous tale of <s>Rāma</s>'s valor.
Then <s>Śauri</s>, drawing near with his followers, saw the son of the divine river
lying on his bed of arrows, as though enveloped by a net of his own rays.
His body was like the young sun, aged, yet with aged and deepened splendor,
enclosed like a lion in a broad golden cage of arrows.
Descending from his chariot, <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, and <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s> with his followers,
all bowed down, sat nearby, and praised the grandsire.
Then the lotus-eyed one respectfully addressed the son of <s>Śāntanu</s>,
who was painfully pierced by rows of arrows, as if cooling him with his gaze:
"I hope your stainless knowledge, the supreme vision of <s>brahman</s>,
is not being lost, though you are sewn through with arrows cruel as thunderbolt-points.
You are a storehouse of gemlike virtues, the crest-jewel of men endowed with valor;

children.text: dhanyatā māninī manye vahati tvāṃ vasuṃdharā ||
children.translated_text: I think the earth bears you as a <s>Vasu</s>, proud of her own blessedness.
O hero, as you are tormented by arrows, the son of <s>Dharma</s>, scorched by deep remorse,

children.text: vyathito dharmatanayo na kvāpi labhate dhṛtim ||
children.translated_text: is distressed and nowhere finds any firmness of mind.
All-knowing one, tell him all the <s>dharmas</s> at my word;
with your faculties serene and your knowledge keen, become free from pain."
Having spoken thus, the blessed lord who sleeps on the Milk Ocean, he whose banner bears <s>Garuḍa</s>,
removed the pain of the man of divine vows with the nectar of his hand.
Then a shower of flowers fell on the heads of <s>Gāṅgeya</s> and <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>,
and <s>Vyāsa</s>, <s>Nārada</s>, and the foremost sages praised the two with smiles.
When he had said, "Tomorrow I shall speak all the <s>dharmas</s>," then <s>Janārdana</s>,
having taken leave of the son of <s>Jāhnavī</s>, set out together with the <s>Pāṇḍavas</s>.
After <s>Śauri</s> and the sons of <s>Pṛthā</s> had spent the night in their own lodging,

children.text: rathaiḥ śāntanavaṃ draṣṭuṃ prātaḥ sarve samāyayuḥ ||
children.translated_text: they all came together in the morning by chariot to see the son of <s>Śāntanu</s>.
Quickly leaving their chariots, they bowed down to the grandsire
and sat surrounding him as he was attended by the great seers.
Then <s>Hari</s>, having inquired after <s>Bhīṣma</s>, whose pain was quieted and who was free from illness,
said, "Learned one, let the duties proper to each station be told to the son of <s>Dharma</s>."
"By your grace I have attained my purpose; I shall speak at your command.

children.text: kiṃ tu pṛcchatu māṃ rājā dharmaniṣṭho yudhiṣṭhiraḥ ||
children.translated_text: But let King <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, steadfast in <s>dharma</s>, question me."

children.text: vṛtte kṣatrocite kārye na lajjā kartumarhati
children.translated_text: "When a task proper to a kṣatriya has been done, one ought not feel shame."
When the grandsire had spoken thus, <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, at <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>'s words,
approached and bowed to <s>Bhīṣma</s>'s feet, his face bent down with modesty.

children.text: sa tena mūrdhnyupāghrāya pṛccha māmiti coditaḥ ||
children.translated_text: After <s>Bhīṣma</s> had smelled his head and urged him, "Question me,"

children.text: prajānāṃ pālane dharmaṃ pūrvaṃ papraccha dharmajaḥ
children.translated_text: the son of <s>Dharma</s> first asked about <s>dharma</s> in the protection of subjects.

children.text: tato jagāda gāṅgeyaḥ praṇamya manasā harim ||
children.translated_text: Then <s>Gāṅgeya</s>, bowing in his mind to <s>Hari</s>, spoke:

children.text: śṛṇu putra yathā rājye virājante nareśvarāḥ
children.translated_text: "Listen, son, to how kings shine in sovereignty.
For the negligent, rulership is a supreme seat of uncertainty.
The ornament of kings, surpassing bracelets, armlets, and necklaces,
is constant respect for the twice-born and the protection and pleasing of the subjects.
Brahmins are the supreme divinity for punishment and favor alike;

children.text: rājñāṃ śriyo hi tadvākyādbhavanti na bhavanti ca ||
children.translated_text: for the fortunes of kings exist or do not exist according to their word.
Royal power is born from the brahmin, as fire is from water,
and a weapon from stone; these meet destruction in their own sources.

children.text: rājavṛttiriyaṃ pūrvā yanna tīvraṃ na mārdavam
children.translated_text: This is the ancient way of royal conduct: it is neither severe nor soft.
Like the ocean, terrible with swelling poison and nectar, it is nevertheless to be served.
The wealth of kings is guarded by servants who are beneficial and honorable,
yet unrestrained kings do not show regard even for those very men.
Good policy is the natural ornament of royal ways, and discipline of the wealth of virtues,
just as loveliness is the ornament of women.
He is a king in whose lotus-like ears, the playground of fortune,
slanderers do not make men of established livelihood objects of contempt.
For earth-rulers who have restrained minds and possess the strength of good counsel,
success lies in taking hold of every mind, just as it does for yogins.
Always gentle like a child, free from faint-heartedness, fond of recreation,
Servants regard as mere straw a king who is given to laughter and joking.
Having obtained the intimacy of jesting counsel with a light-minded king,
they overstep one boundary after another and behave as they please.
They approach the king's women, adorned with ornaments equal to the king's,

children.text: suṣiraṃ kurvate rājyaṃ svāṃ khaniṃ mūṣikā iva ||
children.translated_text: and hollow out the kingdom like mice hollowing their own mine.

children.text: hayaṃ rathaṃ gajaṃ vāso rājayogyaṃ tathāsanam
children.translated_text: Taking a horse, a chariot, an elephant, clothing, and likewise a seat fit for a king,

children.text: āruhya rājñā spardhante vismaranti ca bhṛtyatām ||
children.translated_text: they rival the king and forget that they are servants.

children.text: bahu dattaṃ na manyante yācante durlabhānyapi
children.translated_text: They do not think that much has been given, and they ask even for things hard to obtain;
they criticize their master's private conduct and scatter secret counsel abroad.
They take what is due from the king and shrink from their own proper duties,
and they falsely proclaim in the world that the king is subject to their control.
When their master is attached to play, they gradually discern his vulnerable points;
what else? The king's favorites, with clever minds, play with him.
Spirits may be pacified by spells, and death may be turned back by gifts;

children.text: prajānāṃ dalane saktā na tu te rājasaṃmatāḥ ||
children.translated_text: but those favored by the king, when intent on crushing the subjects, are not so restrained.
A king with good allies, firm in undertaking, secret in counsel, and always ready,
beneficial to his subjects and vigilant, shines in his kingdom.

children.text: ko hi paśyedimaṃ lokaṃ gāḍhena tamasā vṛtam
children.translated_text: Who indeed could see this world, covered in dense darkness,

children.text: rājñaḥ śaśāṅkayaśasaḥ pratāpo yadi na sphuret ||
children.translated_text: if the majesty of the king, whose fame is moonlike, did not shine forth?
In this mud of the Kali age, <s>dharma</s>, standing on one foot,
would inevitably stumble without leaning on the kings' <s>daṇḍa</s> (punitive authority).
Long ago, when the world was without a king and the overthrow of <s>dharma</s> had begun,
<s>Brahmā</s>, entreated by the gods, set himself to the means of polity.
From the <s>śāstra</s> whose fruit is the four aims of life, with portions taken by the chief sages,
he created from his mind a mighty, stainless son, <s>Jiṣṇu</s>.
Appointed by the Blessed One to protect the subjects,
he disregarded that command and withdrew, intent on renunciation.
Though praised, his son likewise went away to austerity;
and his son, named <s>Kardama</s>, dispassionate, went to the forest.
Thereafter from the son of <s>Anaṅga</s> there was born a very powerful son;
he became king and took as wife the daughter of <s>Mṛtyu</s>, dear to the sages.

children.text: venaṃ nāma sutaṃ tasyāṃ samprāpya tapase yayau
children.translated_text: Having obtained from her a son named <s>Vena</s>, he went away to austerity;
then King <s>Vena</s> became cruel, swollen with the poison of anger.
The sages killed him with mantra-purified kuśa grasses, sharp as thunderbolts;
then those great seers churned his right thigh with mantras.
They saw a short-bodied, deformed man arisen from it;
when they told him, 'Sit down,' he became the progenitor of the <s>Niṣādas</s>.

children.text: venasya dakṣiṇaṃ pāṇiṃ nirmathya munayaḥ punaḥ
children.translated_text: Again the sages churned <s>Vena</s>'s right hand,
and saw the joyful <s>Vainya</s>, armed and possessed of <s>Śakra</s>'s valor.
Having obtained <s>daṇḍanīti</s> (the policy of punishment), he ruled at the sages' command
the very earth that had come to him, jewel-giving and complete with mountains and oceans.
The Blessed <s>Hari</s>, companion of the world-protectors, entered him;
from then onward rulers of the earth have been known as gods among men.
When that king, shining with royal virtues, governed the earth,
the subjects remained intent on their own <s>dharma</s>, because of proper fear of punishment.
By him this bearing of the <s>daṇḍa</s> was established for the stability of kings,

children.text: yathā lokāḥ prakāśante na sūryeṇa na cendunā ||
children.translated_text: by which the worlds are illumined, not by the sun and not by the moon.
When a king devoted to <s>dharma</s> has rightly resolved to protect the subjects,
the settled orders born from the division of the four <s>varṇas</s> are not destroyed.
For those who proceed according to rule from one <s>āśrama</s> to another,
the attainment prescribed by the four-<s>āśrama</s> system is not ruined by obstacles.
In ancient times, when King <s>Māndhātṛ</s> desired to behold a sacrifice,
the Blessed <s>Viṣṇu</s> himself came by his own māyā, taking the form of <s>Śakra</s>.

children.text: pṛṣṭo jijñāsayā tena sa rājā praṇipatya tam
children.translated_text: When he was questioned in inquiry by that king, who bowed before him,
he spoke of the foundation of all <s>dharmas</s>, for the pacification of royal rule.
Through royal policy the subjects always proceed in their own duties;
the conduct of the king is the cause of <s>śruti</s>, <s>smṛti</s>, and good custom.
Because the lord of men is the protector of this path of <s>dharma</s>,
out of respect he considered him, established in his own <s>dharma</s>, equal to himself.
The king is the father of the subjects; the world sinks when there is no king.
Good people may live even among mlecchas, but not in a kingless land.

children.text: durbalaṃ ghnanti balinaḥ sevante ca parastriyaḥ
children.translated_text: The strong kill the weak and approach others' wives;
in a realm bereft of a king, people eat one another's flesh.
Formerly, subjects without a king, sunk in the overthrow of order,
made <s>Manu Vaivasvata</s> their king for the sake of the royal share.
Long ago King <s>Sumanas</s>, son of <s>Kausalya</s>, questioned <s>Bṛhaspati</s>;
he described the bearer of the <s>daṇḍa</s> as the supreme refuge of the worlds.
In kingdoms without a king, Fire does not carry the oblation,

children.text: na ca dharmāḥ pravartante na ca varṣati vāsavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: nor do <s>dharmas</s> proceed, nor does <s>Vāsava</s> send rain.

children.text: kuto dhanaṃ kuto dārāḥ śarīraṃ ca kuto nṛṇām
children.translated_text: How can there be wealth, how wives, and how even men's bodies,
so long as the earth-lord, the protector made of all the gods, does not exist?
The king is the sun in seeing all, <s>Yama</s> in restraining sinners,
<s>Kubera</s> in maintenance, and Fire in acts of expiation.
One who seizes royal wealth, one who kills, or even one who tolerates such an offender,
all go to hell, like those who steal a brahmin's property.
Of sacrificers, of those whose conduct is righteous, and of those who have laid down action through dispassion,
the king obtains an equal fruit by protecting the worlds.
Having heard this speech of the preceptor of the gods, that king

children.text: ciraṃ prajāḥ svadharmasthāḥ pālayitvā divaṃ yayau ||
children.translated_text: protected his subjects, who remained established in their own <s>dharma</s> (duty), for a long time and went to heaven.
A vigilant king, not revealing to enemies any loss in treasury, fortress, army, and the like,
should always secure support and refuge for himself.
For kings whose counsels are guarded on every side, whose eyes are hidden agents,
and whose strength lies in sound constituent powers, royal fortune is imperishable.
Free from hatred, he should practice <s>dharmas</s>; gentle, he should give up partial attachment.
Not harsh, he should acquire wealth; pursuing desire, he should not be puffed up with pride.
He should speak what is pleasing without being abject, and be bold without boasting.
He should show compassion and generosity without selfish desire, and be skillful without bitter speech.

children.text: maittraḥ syād akhalāsaṅgī yudhyeta na tu bandhubhiḥ
children.translated_text: He should be friendly, not attached to rogues; he should fight, but not with kinsmen.
He should strike enemies with many weapons, yet in all things avoid needless violence.
He should impart knowledge, but not to the wicked; he should praise virtues, but not his own.
He should take wealth, but not from the good; he should not resort to evil men.
He should punish, but not without inquiry; he should deliberate, but not in open assembly.
He should not enrich misers, and he should not place trust in enemies.
He should protect his wives without jealousy, and be accomplished in the arts without deceit.
He should enjoy beloved women, but not excessively; he should eat wholesome food, not what is harmful.

children.text: sevetārcyānna tu stabdho bhavecchiṣyo na māyayā
children.translated_text: He should attend upon those worthy of honor without arrogance, and become a pupil without guile.
He should worship the gods, but not from ostentation; he should desire blameless prosperity.
He should cultivate affection without excessive submissiveness, and be capable without rashness.

children.text: āśāṃ sṛjenna viphalāṃ vibhajeta na niṣṭhuram ||
children.translated_text: He should not create fruitless hope, and he should not distribute shares cruelly.
He should be one who strikes, but not everywhere; he should kill enemies, but not exterminate them without remainder.
He should not become angry at the faultless; he should be gracious, but not toward enemies.
Endowed with such virtues, kings born in the lineage of <s>Pṛthu</s>
go on, bright with fame, constantly becoming a necklace for royal fortune.

children.text: brāhmaṇāḥ sarvadā rājñā mūrdhni kāryā bubhūṣatā
children.translated_text: Brahmins must always be placed upon the head by a king who wishes to prosper,

children.text: brāhmeṇa tejasā yuktaṃ balaṃ kṣātraṃ hi duḥsaham ||
children.translated_text: for kṣatriya power joined with brahminical splendor is hard to withstand.

children.text: aiḍena bhūbhujā pṛṣṭaḥ purā provāca mārutaḥ
children.translated_text: Long ago, when questioned by the king <s>Aiḍa</s>, <s>Māruta</s> declared:

children.text: brāhmaṇānāmiyaṃ pṛthvī dhanaṃ vā jātu rakṣitam ||
children.translated_text: 'This earth, and wealth too when it is guarded, belong in truth to the brahmins.'
Therefore a lord of the earth, without first presenting the land to the brahmins,
does not deserve to enjoy at will even what he himself has gained, though he is heroic.
A king joined with a brahmin household priest, a maker of fearlessness for all the worlds,
becomes a victor over enemies and over every good fortune.

children.text: mucukundaḥ purā rājā vijitya sakalā diśaḥ
children.translated_text: Long ago King <s>Mucukunda</s>, after conquering all the quarters,
went in his might to conquer <s>Kubera</s>, the friend of <s>Rudra</s>.
Then, when battle began, the powerful <s>Guhyakas</s>

children.text: pṛthunā mucukundasya tejasā ca kṣayaṃ yayuḥ
children.translated_text: were destroyed by the vast splendor of <s>Mucukunda</s>,
and in a moment those heroic <s>Yakṣas</s> and <s>Rākṣasas</s> could not perceive his counsel.

children.text: tataḥ prāptāḥ kubereṇa dattāṃ vasumatīṃ nṛpaḥ
children.translated_text: Then the mighty king, though he had received the earth given by <s>Kubera</s>,
rejected it and seized it by his own valor alone.
Thus royal power, always animated by brahminical power,
possesses the fortune of victory over the three worlds, with its favor unbroken.
Placing brahmins before him, the king should protect his subjects by <s>dharma</s>.
A king receives a fourth share of the merit and sin of his subjects.
For him whose counsel is concealed, who watches over the affairs of his subjects,
who is generous and compassionate, <s>dharma</s> is nowhere lost.
Brahmins who follow the conduct prescribed for them are always to be honored by the king;
but those devoid of proper conduct, fit for harsh punishment, are to be punished like śūdras.
Long ago, when the king of <s>Kekaya</s> was seized by a <s>Rākṣasa</s> in the forest,
he, an ocean of firmness, reassured his own mind and said:

children.text: na bhetavyaṃ tvayā citta rāṣṭre me nāsti viplavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'You need not be afraid, my mind; there is no disorder in my kingdom.

children.text: nāyajvā na vikarmastho na pāpī na kulacyutaḥ
children.translated_text: In my city there is no one who does not sacrifice, no one standing in forbidden conduct,
no sinner, and no one fallen from his family, since I stand in kṣatriya <s>dharma</s>.'

children.text: iti bruvāṇaṃ nṛpatiṃ sa tatyāja niśācaraḥ
children.translated_text: When the king spoke thus, that night-roaming demon released him.
Those whose character is truthful and who stand in their own <s>dharma</s> do not meet defeat.

children.text: viśvasenna ca sarvatra na ca śaṅketa pārthivaḥ
children.translated_text: A king should not trust everywhere, and he should not be suspicious either.

children.text: viśvāsī cātiśaṅkī ca sarvathā vipadāṃ padam ||
children.translated_text: One who is trusting and one who is overly suspicious are, in every way, seats of calamities.

children.text: āpteṣvapi na viśvāsaḥ kartavyaḥ kila bhūbhujā
children.translated_text: A king, indeed, should not place trust even in reliable men,

children.text: na śarīrāṇi cetāṃsi sthirāṇi na hi dehinām ||
children.translated_text: for neither bodies nor minds are stable among embodied beings.
Therefore treasury and counsel must be guarded carefully,
and at the proper times they must be inspected by the vigilant king himself.
Long ago the venerable one whose banner bears <s>Garuḍa</s> said to <s>Nārada</s>:
'I bear the burden of anxiety over the daily affairs of the kings of the <s>Vṛṣṇis</s>.
Endowed with virtue and valor, proud as they are, they do not heed me;

children.text: na śṛṇvanti na manyante girā māṃ vyathayanniva ||
children.translated_text: they do not listen and do not respect me, and they seem to wound me with their words.'
Hearing this, the divine sage replied to <s>Keśava</s>:
'Great souls, rich in strength of character, do indeed bear the business of a clan.
By generosity, patience, power, gentleness, and honesty,
the greatly virtuous remain under the control of the steadfast, bound by their virtues.
But those who understand wealth do not praise straightforwardness in treasuries.'
Hearing this said by <s>Nārada</s>, <s>Hari</s> replied, 'So be it.'
A lord of men should entrust affairs to ministers who are wholly pure,
only after always learning their conduct through spies.

children.text: kośādhyakṣaḥ svayaṃ rājā parirakṣyaḥ śuciḥ sadā
children.translated_text: The king himself should always carefully guard a pure superintendent of the treasury,

children.text: amātyā na sahante taṃ goptāraṃ kośahāriṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: for ministers who steal the treasury do not tolerate him as its guardian.
Formerly, in the city of <s>Kṣemadarśin</s>, lord of <s>Kosala</s>,
The sage <s>Kālakavṛkṣīya</s>, having arrived by chance, stayed there.
Carrying a crow in a cage, he called it the king of all birds,
and as he moved about he learned everything about the conduct of those living from the king.
The eavesdropping on counsel, improper acts, and loss of treasury by the ministers

children.text: sa nivedya sadā rājñe pratyakṣaṃ samadarśayat ||
children.translated_text: he always reported to the king and showed directly before his eyes.

children.text: te sarve kaṇṭakaṃ matvā saṃhatya nṛpajīvinaḥ
children.translated_text: All those royal dependents, thinking him a thorn, banded together

children.text: suptaṃ taṃ vāyasaṃ rātrau jaghnurbāṇena nirjane ||
children.translated_text: and at night, in a lonely place, killed the sleeping crow with an arrow.
Seeing the crow slain, the sage came to the king and said,
"Farewell, O king; I am going away from fear of your dependents.

children.text: sa tairme nihataḥ kākaḥ prāha yo māṃ bhava dvitam
children.translated_text: That crow of mine has been killed by them, the one who spoke to me as your second self.
The crow fell by fate; the arrow was loosed for my sake.
After piercing, it will cast down the ministers." Having said this, he ceased.

children.text: rājāpi tadgirā kāle śoṣayitvā krameṇa tān
children.translated_text: In time, by that speech, the king gradually dried those men up,

children.text: dānena bhedayitvā ca cakre niṣkaṇṭakāṃ śriyam ||
children.translated_text: and by splitting them with gifts he made his fortune free of thorns.
Therefore a king should appoint, in due succession, a watcher beneficial to himself,
from fear of whom all the scribes and officials become divided in their coalition.
There should be one superintendent over a hundred chiefs of servants,
and an overseer over a thousand of them; he should report everything to the king.
Officials devour hamlet, village, city, and kingdom
if the wise do not appoint inspectors above them, one over another,
and they deserve harsh correction, for they are hard to restrain when their corruption has ripened fiercely.
With sighing marks, erasures, and inverted sequences of writing,
who is able to expose the theft of these hired bellows?
For those whose way of life is plunder, who delight in starting and smoothing over yawns,
entire cities are only a mouthful as their words sink down the pit of the throat.
One should protect the earth as it is being manipulated by them with ghost-like movements,
for their crooked state ends in the terrible torments of hell.
Formerly the sage <s>Utathya</s> spoke to King <s>Yauvanāśva</s>:
"O king, in protecting the earth, undertake the removal of thorns.
One should protect the helpless and the weak and show compassion to the miserable,
for the fortunes of kings are destroyed at the root by the cries of the miserable.
Even wealth becomes misfortune for kings through oppression of the people;
how can the creeper of prosperity endure the axe of public reproach?
A king becomes generous, furnished with counselors, heroic, grateful, truthful, eloquent,
and noble-born through the good deeds of his subjects.
When this had been said by <s>Utathya</s>, the lord of the earth <s>Māndhātā</s>

children.text: tathā śaśāsa yaśasā yathā jīvanniva sthitaḥ ||
children.translated_text: ruled in such a way through his fame that he remained as if still living.
Long ago the sage <s>Vāmadeva</s> spoke to the lord of <s>Kosala</s>:
"Through lapse of <s>dharma</s>, the fortunes of kings suddenly diminish.
By friends won through affection, by wise men won through honor,
and likewise by servants won through wealth, the prosperity of kings is sustained.

children.text: śṛṇoti karuṇākrandaṃ śrutvā ca trāyate bhayāt
children.translated_text: He hears the compassionate cry, and having heard it, rescues from fear;

children.text: nāvicārya sṛjeddaṇḍaṃ yaḥ sa sarvapriyo nṛpaḥ ||
children.translated_text: the king who does not inflict punishment without inquiry is dear to all.
There is no greater cause of sin for a king than this:
that his subjects become estranged, like women from a bad husband.
Hearing what had thus been said by <s>Vāmadeva</s>, that lord of the earth,
abiding in his own <s>dharma</s>, became dear to his subjects.
A kṣatriya who does not fight those in a difficult position, unprepared,

children.text: na yudhyate kṣatriyo yaḥ sa dharmavijayī nṛpaḥ ||
children.translated_text: with exhausted armies and stricken by fear, is a king victorious by <s>dharma</s>.

children.text: tathā manye na śocyaḥ śvā mṛto viṇmūtrakardame
children.translated_text: So too, I think, a dog dead in a mire of excrement and urine is not so pitiable
as a kṣatriya struck down on a bed before his own people.
When the army has been torn apart by enemies and the servants have been killed before them,
those who themselves depart in safety: shame on those disgraces among kṣatriyas!

children.text: yasya pṛṣṭhaṃ na paśyanti yudhyamānasya śatravaḥ
children.translated_text: The king whose back enemies do not see while he is fighting,

children.text: sa hataḥ svargamāsādya śakreṇa spardhate nṛpaḥ ||
children.translated_text: when slain, reaches heaven and rivals <s>Śakra</s>.

children.text: ambarīṣaḥ purā rājā yajvā prāpya surālayam
children.translated_text: Long ago King <s>Ambarīṣa</s>, a sacrificer, reached the abode of the gods
and saw his army-leader named <s>Sudeva</s>, greater than himself in splendor.
As he went higher and higher above all those rich in merit,

children.text: taṃ dṛṣṭvā vismitaḥ śakraṃ papraccha sa mahīpatiḥ ||
children.translated_text: the earth-lord, seeing him with amazement, asked <s>Śakra</s>:
"Having protected the earth according to <s>dharma</s> and according to scripture,

children.text: iṣṭvā dattvā ca taptvā ca prāpto 'haṃ tvatpurīmimām ||
children.translated_text: having sacrificed, given gifts, and practiced austerity, I have reached this city of yours.
By what act does this general of mine, <s>Sudeva</s>,
stand so high, like the sun, overpowering us with his rays?"
Thus questioned by the king, the lord of the gods replied to him:
"Listen, O king, by what this commander is greater than you.
In the sacrificial fire of weapons, in the battle-sacrifice, with blood as ghee and bows as ladles,
with headless trunks as sacrificial posts, this accomplished man offered his own body.
This hero shines, encircled by his radiance,
unshaken in battle and granting fearlessness to those whose severed limbs have fallen.
Hearing this, the king, amazed and praising heroic prowess,
astonished and delighted, honored him in his mind.
Asked long ago by the lord of the gods about royal policy, <s>Bṛhaspati</s>

children.text: uvāca śrīryathā rājñāṃ na karoti taḍidbhramam ||
children.translated_text: spoke of how the prosperity of kings should not become a mere flash of lightning:
"By sweet speech alone one should bring about the root-destruction of an enemy;

children.text: ghoreṇa kalahenāpto jaghanyo hi jayaḥ smṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: for victory gained through a dreadful quarrel is remembered as the lowest kind.
A weapon drawn for an uncertain result, and a battle of words, merely dry up the throat.
One should kill an enemy with pleasing words, as a hunter kills a deer.
Knowing place and time, one should bow to a powerful enemy who is rising up;
and at the proper time, when he has declined, one should kill that very enemy. This is the sequence of policy.

children.text: sāmnā seveta balinaṃ lubdhaṃ dānena sādhayet
children.translated_text: One should attend upon the strong with conciliation, and subdue the greedy with gifts;
one should bring down an angry minister by division, and an inferior foe by punishment.
An enemy who is careless, together with his army, should be assessed by treasury, fortress, and strength;
and one who is bereft of every expedient should quietly be subjected to punishment.
He should always watch his own dependents who have grown disaffected,
conceal his own weak points from them, and consider the weak point of his enemy.

children.text: na bhāṣate vepate ca lakṣitaḥ kṣmāṃ nirīkṣate
children.translated_text: When he is noticed, a disaffected man does not speak, trembles, and looks at the ground;
a person whose heart has turned away is not won even by a gift of four-footed beasts.
Hearing this spoken by his teacher, the glorious <s>Puraṃdara</s>
became always attentive, guarding himself and searching out others.
A lord of the earth should not grieve over misfortune that has come by fate;
by freedom from despondency, even lost fortunes are recovered.
Long ago the sage <s>Kālakavṛkṣīya</s>, skilled in policy, when asked by the king <s>Kṣemadarśin</s>
after that ruler had fallen from power, spoke as follows.
O king, even the fortunes of the gods are unsteady as the play of lightning,
and life is not eternal, for whose sake you seek royal fortune.

children.text: tathāpi yadi te vāñchā sve rājye śatruṇā hate
children.translated_text: Still, if you have a desire for your own kingdom, which has been struck down by an enemy,

children.text: gatvā tameva sevasva maunaṃ kṛtvā kṛtāñjaliḥ ||
children.translated_text: go and serve that very enemy, keeping silence and holding your hands joined in reverence.
Become his servant for so long, in every way patient under hardship,
until you are gradually built up in treasury and in allies.

children.text: praviśya ca manaḥ prītyā priyavādī yathā tathā
children.translated_text: Having entered into his confidence by affection, speaking pleasantly in whatever way is needed,
you should encourage the enemy in improper undertakings that are difficult to overcome.
Then, when he has fallen into uncertainty, his treasury drained and himself careless,
you should make him fit to be dealt with in a moment by those various means, or by wealth.
When the sage had spoken thus, the king, bent away from base conduct,
proud and radiant with noble birth, said, 'I will not do this.'
Then, perceiving the truthful disposition of that king,

children.text: dūto bhūtvā svayaṃ saṃdhau tasya śatrumayo 'jayat ||
children.translated_text: the sage himself became an envoy for his treaty and won over his enemy.
Making peace with <s>Kṣemadarśin</s> through the sage's words, the <s>Vaideha</s> king

children.text: vitatāra sutāṃ tasmai vibhavaṃ ca yathocitam ||
children.translated_text: gave his daughter to him, and wealth as was fitting.
A king should protect his own faction and split the faction of others;

children.text: samyagvṛttena satyena vartante hi gaṇāḥ sadā ||
children.translated_text: for factions always persist through proper conduct and truth.
A king wins through factions when they are thoughtfully cared for and maintained by him;
when they are neglected, even if united, he quickly comes to ruin through those very factions.

children.text: praśāmyati bahiḥ kopo rājñāṃ sāmādibhiḥ kṣaṇāt
children.translated_text: The outward anger of kings is calmed in a moment by conciliation and the other means;
but anger arising within a faction, hidden like fire in a house, has no end.

children.text: daivataṃ pitaro yasya dharmo yasya prajāhitam
children.translated_text: He whose divinity and ancestors are honored, whose <s>dharma</s> is the welfare of his subjects,

children.text: samyagdaṇḍo vrataṃ yasya sa rājā yajvanāṃ varaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and whose vow is proper punishment, that king is the best of sacrificers.

children.text: na satyaṃ kevalaṃ satyamanṛtaṃ na tathānṛtam
children.translated_text: Truth alone is not truth, and falsehood is not always falsehood;
what is beneficial to all the world is truth; the rest is otherwise.
A king, it is said, should treat a man of false conduct with falsehood,
and one who is true in character should be served with truth by one who desires prosperity.
Kings who sacrifice, whose intentions are pure, who are generous and shower gifts on worthy recipients,
who protect all forms of <s>dharma</s> and perform meritorious deeds,
who listen to the words of the good and break those who steal wealth,
cross over terrible difficulties both here and in the next world.
Those devoted to <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, of good conduct, joined with austerity, peaceful, and truthful in speech,
also cross over difficulties.
Men in the world may be harsh though gentle in conduct, soft though cruel in action;

children.text: bhavanti puruṣā loke tāṃśca budhyeta bhūmipaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and a king should understand them.
Long ago there was a king named <s>Preraka</s>, lord of <s>Pūrikā</s>,
a dreadful, low man, acting like an eater of flesh.

children.text: kālena pañcatāṃ yātaḥ sa ca prāptaḥ śṛgālatām
children.translated_text: In time he died and became a jackal;
by merits performed in a former birth, he sorrowfully remembered his birth.
Having fallen into a despised creation, his mind wearied by disgust,
he ate fruit and did not take meat even when it was brought by others.
Seeing him, a pure-vowed one living in the cremation ground,
all the jackals angrily spoke, condemning his strange conduct:
'Though you live in this cremation ground, you, dull-witted one, have abandoned
this delicious elixir of meat, because of a foolish vow.
All this inversion torments the hearts of the good:
that in this dreadful ancestral grove a jackal does not eat meat.
When they told him, 'Eat,' he, whose intention was stainless, replied:
'Birth is not the cause of character, nor is a religious order the cause of merit.
Do they not declare the killing of living beings to be a sin in a religious order?

children.text: manaḥ śuddhikṛtaṃ sarvaṃ pramāṇaṃ karma dehinām ||
children.translated_text: For embodied beings, every deed made by purity of mind is authoritative.'

children.text: iti bruvāṇaṃ taṃ sarve vijñāya dṛḍhaniścayam
children.translated_text: When he spoke thus, all of them recognized his firm resolve,
and said nothing out of resentment, but merely burned with anger.
Then one day, hearing of his conduct, a tiger came upon him

children.text: uvāca mama sācivyaṃ śuddhātmā bhajatāṃ bhavān ||
children.translated_text: and said, 'Pure-souled one, let your honor enter my service as minister.'
Then the jackal, hearing that, bowed with humility and said:

children.text: svācchandyamamṛtaṃ tyaktvā kaḥ sevāṃ vikaṭāṃ śrayet ||
children.translated_text: 'Who would abandon the nectar of independence and resort to harsh service?
Who would abandon the wealth of contentment, effortless and imperishable,
and ask for service stained by the terror of dependence on fate?
Or else, if because of your insistence I do what your honor says...
You must always have me alone as your servant,
devoted in loyalty, taking refuge in you alone, and not living among a faction.

children.text: vināśayanti piśunā na yathā māṃ tathā kṛthāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Do not act so that slanderers destroy me, as they otherwise would.
Having spoken thus, the one whose nature was peace, free from desire and out of reverence for what deserved honor,
accepted the office of minister to that tiger, who said, 'So be it.'
When the tiger had reassured him, brought him to earth, and made him the sole chief over all,
his dependents, seeing it, fell into an ocean of grief.
They took the meat prepared for the tiger to the jackal's dwelling.

children.text: kva māṃsamiti te pṛṣṭā vyāghreṇa kṣudrakāriṇaḥ
children.translated_text: When the tiger asked them, 'Where is the meat?', those petty wrongdoers
said, 'It has been stolen and carried off by your pure minister.'

children.text: mithyācāraṃ viditvā taṃ dṛṣṭvā māṃsaṃ ca tadgṛhe
children.translated_text: Learning of that false conduct and seeing the meat in his house,
the tiger, blinded by anger and wishing to kill him, came in a rage.
Then the tigress, his mother, suspecting slander, approached him and said:

children.text: śuddhāya tasmai bhṛtyāya vimohātputra mā krudhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'My son, do not in delusion be angry with that servant, who is pure.

children.text: bahavaḥ saṃhatā dhūrtāḥ saṃmataṃ sacivaṃ navam
children.translated_text: Many rogues, joined together, smear a newly approved minister,
though innocent, with a false fault, petty men who think themselves clever.

children.text: svarūpaṃ vikṛto dveṣṭi śūraṃ bhīrurbudhaṃ jaḍaḥ
children.translated_text: The deformed hate beauty; the coward hates the brave; the dullard hates the wise;

children.text: kulīnaṃ hīnajanmā ca duḥśīlā ca pativratām ||
children.translated_text: the base-born man hates the noble, and the woman of bad conduct hates the faithful wife.
Thus awakened by his mother, and having investigated the truth through spies,
the tiger understood that he was pure, won him over, and became ashamed.
Then the jackal said to him, 'Farewell, lord; I am going.
Dishonored by you, I cannot bear to remain, since our compact has been abandoned.

children.text: guṇavāniti saṃsatsu yaḥ stutaḥ sādhubhiḥ purā
children.translated_text: One who was formerly praised in assemblies by good men as virtuous
must not again be spoken of otherwise by those whose vows are true, even when there is a fault.
When such a bond has been broken, affection is very hard to restore.'
Having spoken thus and taken leave of the tiger, the jackal went away to practice austerity.
In time, fasting and with the impressions of worldly life pacified,

children.text: vane kalevaraṃ tyaktvā tridivaṃ prayayau kṛtī ||
children.translated_text: that accomplished one abandoned his body in the forest and went to heaven.

children.text: āsthāya vaitasīṃ vṛttiṃ deśakālau samīkṣya ye
children.translated_text: Those who adopt the conduct of the reed, considering place and time,

children.text: na santi tiṣṭhantyuccairvā na te yānti parābhavam ||
children.translated_text: and who are neither absent nor stand too high, do not go to defeat.

children.text: sāgaraḥ saritaḥ sarvāḥ purā papraccha kautukāt
children.translated_text: Long ago the ocean, out of curiosity, asked all the rivers:
'In your currents I see all the trees uprooted.

children.text: ete viśanti māṃ vṛkṣā hṛtāḥ kūlaṃkaṣairjalaiḥ
children.translated_text: These trees enter me, carried off by waters that scour the banks;

children.text: vetasaṃ na tu paśyāmi kasmādatra taṭodbhavam ||
children.translated_text: but I do not see the reed born on the bank. Why is that?'
When the rivers were asked this by the ocean, <s>Jāhnavī</s> said:
'The reed, while being carried away by the waters, always bends down.

children.text: hantuṃ na śakyāste vṛkṣā mahaughairvinamanti ye
children.translated_text: Those trees that bend before great floods cannot be killed;
but other trees, foolish and proud, break from fear itself.'
Hearing this speech of the <s>Ganges</s>, the lord of rivers said, 'So it is,'

children.text: mene ca vaitasīṃ vṛttiṃ śreyase deśakālayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: and considered the conduct of the reed best for success according to place and time.
The wealth of kings is their own intelligence; so too is skill for those endowed with energy.
The lazy and the unintelligent are in every way a seat of calamities.
Long ago a camel, through intense austerity and by a boon from <s>Prajāpati</s>,
obtained a neck a hundred yojanas long, being overcome by laziness.
Then, sitting in one place, with that neck among the pilu groves,
he always maintained his life, thinking it great happiness.
At a time struck by foul weather, one day, by jackals
emaciated with hunger, that long neck, coiled in a circle, was eaten.
A king should appoint to offices men of good family and known conduct.
When wicked men are placed in a high office, they lead only to danger.
A dog, an object of compassion, lived in the hermitage of a certain sage.
Seeing a dreadful leopard one day, he said in fear:
'Blessed one, this hungry leopard has come to kill me.

children.text: pāhi pāhīti tenoktaḥ sa muniḥ karuṇānidhiḥ
children.translated_text: Protect me, protect me!' When he spoke thus, that sage, a treasure of compassion,
said, 'Become equal to this,' and made him have the form of a leopard.
That dog too, having become a leopard and then being terrified by a tiger, again said to the sage,
'Save me,' and by the sage's words he became a tiger.
He too, in time, grew afraid of a rutting elephant, slow with rut,
and, fashioned kindly by the sage, attained the state of a great rutting elephant.
He too, frightened by a five-faced lion with terrible mane,
at once became king of beasts by that sage's command.
Seeing an eight-legged śarabha with great fangs approaching,

children.text: sa viṣaṇṇo munigirā babhūva śarabhaḥ kṣaṇāt ||
children.translated_text: he grew despondent and, by the sage's word, became a śarabha in an instant.
In time, having the form of a śarabha and inspiring fear in all creatures,

children.text: sa jātadarpaḥ sahasā taṃ muniṃ hantumudyayau ||
children.translated_text: he became arrogant and suddenly set out to kill that sage.
Then, destroyed by that sage with a mere roar of 'hūṃ,'
he became again, in an instant, a wretched creature with an impure body.
Thus, by giving prosperity to low men whose character is unknown,
and without considering family and conduct, a king falls into danger.
Knowing such policy, a heroic king should guard this earth,
which yields all desires, by the royal staff, but should not oppress it.
Long ago <s>Vasuhoma</s>, king of <s>Aṅga</s>, on a peak of <s>Himavat</s>,
when questioned by <s>Yauvanāśva</s>, spoke of the origin of punishment.
Formerly a fetus was borne on the head by the creator of creatures for a thousand years.
Suddenly emitted together with a sneeze, that glorious one became <s>Kṣupa</s>.
Meanwhile, the whole world, without the restraint of command,
Seeing this to be without bounds, <s>Prajāpati</s> became distressed.

children.text: athāsya vacasā rudraḥ prayayau daṇḍatāṃ svayam
children.translated_text: Then, at his word, <s>Rudra</s> himself became the <s>daṇḍa</s> (rod of punishment),
fanged, four-armed, blazing, dark in lips and feet, and wearing matted hair.
The god gave it to <s>Viṣṇu</s>; <s>Viṣṇu</s> gave it to <s>Aṅgiras</s>.
He too gave it to <s>Śakra</s> and <s>Marīci</s>; then <s>Marīci</s> gave it to <s>Bhṛgu</s>.

children.text: sa munibhyo dadau te 'pi dikpatibhyo kṣupāya te
children.translated_text: He gave it to the sages; they too gave it to the guardians of the quarters, and they to <s>Kṣupa</s>.
And <s>Kṣupa</s> gave the <s>daṇḍa</s> to <s>Manu</s> for the protection of <s>dharma</s>.
When that pure splendor is properly applied for protection,

children.text: labhante śāśvataṃ vīrā yaśaḥ svargaṃ ca bhūmipāḥ ||
children.translated_text: heroic kings obtain everlasting fame and heaven.
Thus instructed by the king of <s>Aṅga</s>, <s>Māndhātā</s>, lord of the earth,
heard him, his eyes opening wide with joy, and honored him respectfully.
A king's sin born of desire and greed is destroyed by service to brahmins,
by not doing it again, by giving, and by declaring it.

children.text: trayī trātā tato dharmaṃ bhajate tyaktakilbiṣaḥ
children.translated_text: Then, rid of guilt, the protector of the threefold Veda follows <s>dharma</s>.
Thus, when asked long ago by <s>Ariṣṭa</s>, the sage <s>Kāmardaka</s> said:
Character is the ornament of kings, just as good breeding is of learned men.
Through character fortune shines, like a cluster of blossoms through spring.
Seeing your prosperity at the <s>Rājasūya</s>, <s>Duryodhana</s>, shaken by the poison of envy,

children.text: duryodhanaḥ purā pitre dyūte kāmaṃ nyavedayat ||
children.translated_text: formerly told his father of his desire for gambling.
<s>Dhṛtarāṣṭra</s> said to him, 'Son, do not become agitated.
Let sacrifices rich in abundant wealth be undertaken for you too in due course.
If you possess character, you will always obtain fortune greater than that of the sons of <s>Pāṇḍu</s>.

children.text: na hi śīlavataḥ kiṃcidvidyate bhuvi durlabham ||
children.translated_text: For nothing on earth is hard to obtain for a man of character.
Character is, for kings, the moon of the quarters; youth is the captivating ornament
of doe-eyed women, and the month of spring is that of trees.

children.text: videśeṣu dhanaṃ vidyā vyasaneṣu dhanaṃ matiḥ
children.translated_text: In foreign lands learning is wealth; in calamities intelligence is wealth.

children.text: paraloke dhanaṃ dharmaḥ śīlaṃ tu nikhilaṃ dhanam ||
children.translated_text: In the next world <s>dharma</s> is wealth, but character is wealth in its entirety.
Long ago <s>Śakra</s>, seeking the fitting wealth of character,
went with <s>Bṛhaspati</s> before him to <s>Prahlāda</s>, whose power blazed, in the form of a brahmin.
When the lord of the <s>Daityas</s> was humbly asked by him, as by a pupil, 'Tell me the highest good,'
he spoke in due time, his mind intent solely on the welfare of his subjects:
'I have always obtained sovereignty over the three worlds by possessing character.

children.text: śṛṇoti vidyā viduṣāṃ kavīnāṃ saṃśaye vacaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In a matter of doubt, wisdom listens to the words of learned and discerning men.
A thoughtful mind should not hastily accept anything undecided, untouched,
unexplained, or unconsidered, even if it is sweet.
This alone, brahmin, is the welfare of all embodied beings.
But choose a boon; I am pleased by your affectionate service.'
Thus addressed by the lord of the <s>Dānavas</s>, the delighted slayer of <s>Vṛtra</s> said,

children.text: sarvaṃ dehi nijaṃ mahyaṃ śīlaṃ śīlavatāṃ vara ||
children.translated_text: 'Give me all your own character, best of those who possess character.'
Hearing this, the truthful <s>Daitya</s> said to him, 'I give it.'
<s>Śakra</s> too, receiving it by his word, departed wearing the guise of a twice-born.
When that very energetic one had gone, a man like a shadow, of excellent form,
quickly came out from <s>Prahlāda</s>'s body.
Asked then by him, 'Who are you?' he said to the king of the <s>Daityas</s>,
'I am the virtue called character, given away today by you as you wished.'
After saying this, when he had gone to <s>Śakra</s>, another came out after him.
He too, when asked, said to the <s>Daitya</s>, 'I am <s>dharma</s>, who follows the path of character.'
A third also came forth and said to him, 'I am truth.'
Then a fourth came out and said, 'I am wealth.'
A fifth, quickly departing, said, 'I am strength.'
Then <s>Kamalā</s> herself, lotus-eyed and seated on a lotus couch,
came out from <s>Prahlāda</s>'s face and said:
'I am going to the thousand-eyed one, the brahmin who became your pupil.

children.text: tasmai tvayā vitīrṇaṃ hi śīlaṃ śīlavibhūṣaṇa ||
children.translated_text: For to him you have given character, O ornament of character.
From character <s>dharma</s> follows, and truth follows that;

children.text: yātaṃ vittaṃ ca tanmūlaṃ balaṃ caitannibandhanam ||
children.translated_text: wealth, rooted in that, has gone, and strength depends on this.
When these have entered, one after another, the body of the king of the gods,

children.text: śīlāśrayāṃ śriyaṃ viddhi māmapi prasthitāṃ vibho ||
children.translated_text: know that I too, fortune resting on character, am departing, O lord.'
Having spoken thus, <s>Lakṣmī</s> left him and went to <s>Śakra</s>'s abode.
Thus, O <s>Duryodhana</s>, all prosperities arise from character.
Even though he was instructed in this way by the son of <s>Ambikā</s>, <s>Suyodhana</s> did not grow calm.
For those who are bent on death are, through delusion, wholly averse to those worthy of reverence.
Having heard all this, fit for a king, spoken by the grandfather,
and remembering the story of <s>Duryodhana</s>, <s>Dharmaja</s> sighed and said:
'My hope was always very great in regard to the son of <s>Dhṛtarāṣṭra</s>,
that, when we returned from the forest, he would act in that way toward us.
When <s>Janārdana</s> was rejected in every way by him, who desired war,

children.text: āśā viphalatāṃ nītā sā tena mama saṃvṛtā ||
children.translated_text: that hope of mine was made fruitless and blocked by him.
Therefore, when hopes have grown vast, and when they are shattered, how can unbearable sorrows

children.text: nivartante kathaṃ nāma kathyatāṃ me pitāmaha ||
children.translated_text: possibly turn back? Tell me this, grandfather.'
Thus questioned by <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, the son of <s>Śāntanu</s> spoke again:
'Hope, <s>Pārtha</s>, is a very great condition, one that takes away life.
Long ago a <s>Haihaya</s> prince named <s>Sumitra</s>, in a forest,
swiftly pursued a single antelope that was even swifter.
Across level ground, among thickets of trees, through ravines and rugged places,
that archer, following the deer for a very long time, became weary.
Then, reaching an ascetic grove after the deer had again been seen and lost,
Scorched by the destruction of hope, he entered the assembly of sages.
Having bowed to them, he asked about hope, a most painful and very great thing.
A sage named <s>Vṛṣabha</s>, his face smiling, said to him:
Prince, abandon that emaciated hope, which is bound up with suffering.
Formerly King <s>Bhūridyumna</s>, searching for his son named <s>Vīradyumna</s>,
who had been carried off by a horse, came to <s>Badaryāśrama</s>.
Then, reaching the ascetic grove after the animal had been seen and lost again,
scorched by the destruction of hope, he entered the assembly of sages.
Having bowed to them, he asked about hope, a most painful and very great thing.

children.text: munistaṃ vṛṣabho nāma babhāṣe sa smitānanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A sage named <s>Vṛṣabha</s>, his face smiling, said to him:
Prince, abandon that emaciated hope, which is bound up with suffering.
Formerly King <s>Bhūridyumna</s> had a son named <s>Vīradyumna</s>.
There was a sage there named <s>Tanu</s>, tall and of very emaciated form.
Questioned in that painful crisis, he said, 'Do not be distraught, O king.'

children.text: na vidyate janaḥ kaścidāśayā yo na hīyate
children.translated_text: There is no person at all who is not diminished by hope.

children.text: na ca paśyāmi taṃ loke yācakaṃ yo 'bhimanyate ||
children.translated_text: Nor do I see in the world a supplicant whom anyone esteems.
Among the ungrateful, the cruel, the crooked, and the lazy,
hopes become weak, like shallow streams in autumn.
Shame on that still thinner hope, which wastes the body,
when, not obtaining what was promised, it turns back from the heart.

children.text: putre mṛte vā naṣṭe vā piturekātmajasya vā
children.translated_text: When a son is dead or lost, or for a father with only one child,

children.text: āśā dahati gātrāṇi sā kṛśāpi mahīyasī ||
children.translated_text: hope burns the limbs; though slender, she is powerful.
The hopes that old men always have for obtaining sons,

children.text: sthāvire jīrṇakāyānāṃ tāḥ kṛśā api duḥsahāḥ ||
children.translated_text: when their aged bodies are worn out, are unbearable, though slender.
As soon as it is merely gained, hope makes one wander; stretching into the future, slender, it dries one up.
When one is sunk in it, it kills like a tangled snare; shame on hope, giver of death.
Having spoken thus, that sage of divine sight showed the king his son,
and he himself became manifest as the embodiment of <s>dharma</s>.
Having abandoned the nooses of hope, like a yogin who has conquered his senses,
you ought to protect the earth, O <s>Kaunteya</s>, like another <s>Pṛthu</s>.

children.text: kośamūlaṃ balaṃ rājñāṃ tasminkṣīṇe yathā tathā
children.translated_text: The strength of kings has the treasury as its root; when it is depleted, by whatever means,
its increase should be made for the success of <s>dharma</s>, but not with the wealth of Brahmins.
The king asked the son of the heavenly river, the speaker on all <s>dharmas</s>,
about the livelihood of rulers whose treasuries and allies have been exhausted.
When a king has been conquered by the strong, his counsel divided, bereft of refuge,
and fallen through lack of energy, what better course should he resort to?
<s>Bhīṣma</s> said: A weakened king, having made peace with his enemies,
should gradually, with effort, increase his treasury, army, and the rest.

children.text: tūrṇaṃ varteta sāmnā vā tyaktātmā vāraṇaṃ vrajet
children.translated_text: He should act quickly by conciliation, or, abandoning concern for himself, go to battle.
Remaining between the two courses, a procrastinator perishes.
This preservation of the treasury strikes at the root of calamities;
checked by enterprise through it, they are indeed unable to arise.
Vultures indeed go to a corpse, to a burnt piece of charcoal-like wood,
but no one touches a man who is marked by poverty.
Even a corpse wet with a network of veins, putrid and long decayed,

children.text: na tathā varjayantyārād dhanahīnaṃ yathā janam ||
children.translated_text: people do not avoid from afar as much as they avoid a man without wealth.
For those whose minds are bewildered by lost prosperity in a dangerous situation,
<s>maryādā</s> (proper bounds and honor) is imperishable, unassailable wealth.
Even a bandit may be one who has not abandoned proper bounds, not utterly unrestrained.
Proper bounds are the abode of prosperity, just as folly is the abode of calamities.
Formerly the heroic bandit-chief <s>Kopavya</s>, a reverer of elders,
not abandoning proper bounds, attained supreme accomplishment.
He protected those who had laid down their weapons, Brahmins, and likewise women.
Though a friend of all the <s>Dānava</s>s, he obtained great fame.

children.text: na tajjagati nāmāsti yad anākramyam āpadām
children.translated_text: There is nothing at all in the world that is not assailable by calamities.
Protection of the body is first, and intelligence is the remedy for them.
Long ago the fish <s>Prāptajña</s>, <s>Dīrghadarśin</s>, and <s>Dīrghasūtra</s>, with their followers,
having many children, lived in a reservoir.
When the water there was being drained by fishermen who wished to seize them,
<s>Dīrghadarśin</s> said to the others, 'Let us go to another lake.'

children.text: ityarthitau tena yadā tau vimohānna jagmatuḥ
children.translated_text: When those two, though urged by him, did not go because of delusion,

children.text: dīrghadarśī tadā pūrvaṃ svayaṃ prāyātsaraḥ param ||
children.translated_text: <s>Dīrghadarśin</s> then went first by himself to another pond.
Then, when the water had run off and the mass of fish was dragged in by the fishermen,
<s>Prāptajña</s> hung himself on a cord, feigning death.
After killing all the leaping fish and then stringing the others,
the net-living fishermen threw them into another water for washing.
When the unwary fishermen had put them down in the water of the streams,

children.text: alakṣito yayau tūrṇaṃ prāptajño dhīmatāṃ varaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Prāptajña</s>, best of the wise, quickly went away unnoticed.
But <s>Dīrghasūtra</s>, huge-bodied, half alive and writhing,
was killed by a Niṣāda, smashed to pieces with clubs.

children.text: bahūnāṃ gocaraṃ yāto vairiṇāṃ viṣame sthitaḥ
children.translated_text: One who has come within range of many enemies and stands in danger
should make a friend stronger than they are, but should remain very suspicious.
Formerly the mouse <s>Pralaya</s>, dwelling at the root of a banyan tree,
saw a cat named <s>Lomaśa</s> caught in a net.
When that one was bound, the mouse, free from fear, sniffing with restless face,
went about at night for food, scratching the ground with his claws.
He saw a mongoose named <s>Harita</s>, with red face,
and an owl named <s>Candraka</s>, hooting, with terrible eyes.

children.text: tau dṛṣṭvā balinau bhītaḥ samprāpte prāṇasaṃśaye
children.translated_text: Seeing those two strong ones, and frightened when danger to his life had arrived,
the mouse considered every direction and thought for a moment:
"I am afraid of the mongoose and the owl, and the cat is the best of the strong.
For those in a perilous position, when there is uncertainty, alliance with an enemy is protection.
Having decided thus, and with his mind intent on cutting that one's noose,
he spoke to the cat, whose restless eyes shone like blue glass:
"An enemy becomes a friend, and a friend becomes an enemy,

children.text: kālena tasmācchetsyāmi pāśaṃ te mitratāṃ gataḥ ||
children.translated_text: through time; therefore, having become your friend, I will cut your noose."
Hearing this sweet speech, the cat, delighted, made the mouse his friend
and clasped him tightly in his lap, being himself in distress.
Seeing that, the mongoose and the owl, despairing of eating the mouse,
became downcast, fearing that a powerful friendship had arisen.
Then the mouse, very slowly, began to cut the sinew-bond.
The cat kept saying to him, as he delayed, "Quickly, quickly!"
Rogues who, seeking their own interest, cling for a moment by threads of affection,
should be kept waiting, while some part of the task remains, by those whose task they ask to have done.
Reflecting on this with his intelligence, the mouse, skilled in policy, up to the moment of the hunter's arrival,
left him with one part of the noose still remaining.
In the morning, when the fiercer caṇḍāla named <s>Parigha</s> arrived,
armed, living by snares, with his eyes fixed on the net,
the mouse cut the remaining noose and, having cut it, entered his hole.

children.text: yāto vyādho nirāśaśca mārjāre vidrute drutam ||
children.translated_text: The hunter went away disappointed, while the cat swiftly fled.
Freed from that great danger, the cat came to the mouse after some time;
bowing to him as he stayed inside at the door of the hole, he said:

children.text: ahaṃ sa te paraṃ mitram upakāravaśīkṛtaḥ
children.translated_text: "I am that excellent friend of yours, bound by your kindness.
I have become intensely eager for you, my friend; come out from here."
Seeing the cat speaking thus, consecrated as it were for eating him,
with white, sharp-tipped teeth and a face marked by needle-like whiskers,
sniffing the scent of mouse, with eyes half open,
standing still with one foot lifted high, the mouse addressed him:
"Formerly your friendship served me, and I served you.

children.text: gamyatāṃ sa gataḥ kālo na bhūmirvañcaneṣvaham ||
children.translated_text: Go away. That time has passed; I am no ground for deceits.
The sweet words that you speak do not please me today.
That was the time of a petitioner and his need; now there is no association.
Pleasant affectionate speech, polished by regard for one's own purpose,
is what the resolute weak man should recognize from afar in the cruel-minded, whose hearts are far from noble.
Even if, out of gratitude, you might become a friend, your heart is far from noble.
There is no welfare in the meeting of food and eater, for they are opposed."
Having thus rejected the cat with many words, the mouse

children.text: bilaṃ tatyāja kālena dṛṣṭaṃ dhūrtena śatruṇā ||
children.translated_text: in time abandoned that hole, since it had been seen by a crafty enemy.
Thus this policy is to be understood by the wise in alliances with enemies:
one should not trust those who speak pleasantly, especially those who have committed an offense.
Long ago, in the city of <s>Kāmpilya</s>, belonging to King <s>Brahmadatta</s>,
there lived a bird named <s>Pūtanā</s>, a creature that lived by taking life.
Having gained trust in the royal palace, she gave birth to a son,
and a son was born to that king at the same time as her son.
Giving two fruits produced on an island in the ocean,

children.text: svaputraṃ rājaputraṃ ca bālye 'pi balinau vyadhāt ||
children.translated_text: she made both her own son and the prince strong, even in childhood.
Then, one day, the powerful prince took the young bird,
who was absorbed in play, and made him lifeless.
Seeing her son killed, <s>Pūtanā</s> then came near,
and in anger tore out the prince's two eyes with her beak.
Having repaid the injury with an injury, she was grieved and prepared to leave.
As she was going, <s>Brahmadatta</s> looked down from the palace in agitation,
and, seeing his son with his eyes torn out, concealed his dismay and said:
"When wrong has been repaid, enmity has been struck down by enmity.

children.text: kopaḥ sāmyādapakrānto mā gamaḥ putri pūtane ||
children.translated_text: Anger has gone away through equality of return; do not go, daughter <s>Pūtanā</s>."
Hearing this, the bird said, "There is no union now.
Enmity once done and returned becomes doubled through continued association.
An old hostility, even if forgotten, when heard of from teachers and elders,
suddenly becomes new, like fire inside a hollow.
The foolish man who, out of delusion, places trust in one who has injured him,
forgetting himself, suddenly comes under the power of death.
As deer are distressed by song, birds by bait,
and fish by a hook, so men are distressed by being made to trust.
For those split apart by pleasant words, reunion is indeed difficult;
broken pearls are not joined together by little bits of lac.

children.text: dhiktaṃ kudeśaḥ yatrātmā na śete 'śaṅkitaḥ sukham
children.translated_text: Shame on that bad country where one does not sleep happily without fear.

children.text: pravādaḥ kila satyo 'yaṃ yadātmārthe mahīṃ tyajet ||
children.translated_text: That proverb is true: for one's own sake one should abandon the earth itself."

children.text: iti bruvāṇā sā rājñā prārthitāpi punaḥ punaḥ
children.translated_text: Speaking thus, although the king entreated her again and again,
she departed from fear of distrust, abandoning the weight of affection.
In a time of danger, casting aside pity, toward those who have been treated with affection and honor
but have become hostile, one should act with still greater hostility, using intelligence.

children.text: rājñā śatruṃtapākhyena vṛttiṃ nītiṃ ca bhūbhujām
children.translated_text: Long ago, when King <s>Śatruṃtapa</s> asked about the conduct and policy of kings toward enemies,
a sage named <s>Kaṇiṅka</s>, skilled in policy, spoke:
"One should cut an enemy off at the root, or else one should not provoke him.
Otherwise he brings about destruction, like a snake touched by the foot.

children.text: janaṃ viśvasayed vācā śaucaṃ dambhena darśayet
children.translated_text: One should make people trust by speech and display purity by pretense;

children.text: pragāṇaiḥ śapathaiḥ śāstraiḥ śatruṃ seveta śambaraiḥ ||
children.translated_text: One should serve an enemy with loud oaths, scriptures, and spells.
For calming what has passed, with affections, together with dull-witted men and those who have not arrived,
with visible proofs and supporting documents, compacted together, yet without fruit.
Like cotton, he should at once blaze up quickly at some opportune moment;
he should not be, like a fire in wood, of weak heat and marked only by smoke.
For those who seek an advantage, one should always create bonds of expectation through intoxication with hope;
for no one, once the task has been done, gives approval to the doer.
Distress at public reproach, softness, long delay,
or failure to keep one's own counsel are the cutting off of the root of wealth.
For the accomplishment of his own interest he should, at the proper time, be asleep, deaf, or blind;
he should stand like honey on a precipice, hard for all embodied beings to obtain.
He should be harsh, yet sweet in speech, like a stone smeared with molasses;
and he should enter within his enemies like a razor smeared with honey.
He should consider gathering knowledge in order to give the long bait of hope,

children.text: āśāṃ nighnair nimittaiśca hetubhiśca tathā vadet ||
children.translated_text: and should speak of hope with signs that destroy it and with reasons likewise.
So that no delight may come even in a hundred years,
affection that produces dissatisfaction should give men an opening into oneself.
He should be suspicious like a crow and destroy deer-like innocence;
through spies he should become all-knowing, and he should strike his enemy in misfortune.
First he should be one who strikes by deception, and then grieve for the slain as if for his own kinsman;
he should not make a fruitless enmity, nor should he seize anything incomplete.
The needless grinding down of the teeth is chewing dry bone in vain;
having heard this, he should not leave a remnant of an enemy, any more than of a disease.
He should even kill his own son if he obstructs his purpose;
he should be far-seeing like a vulture, and a hypocritical ascetic like a crane.
He should have great energy like a tiger, and be crooked like a serpent;
for the sake of division he should always conciliate the citizens of others.
First he should seduce confederacies, drawing their favorites by wealth;
after producing hostility through learned men, he should not live at ease without suspicion.
Surely, only after understanding all this should one serve a good man.
King <s>Suvera</s>, having heard this spoken by <s>Bhāradvāja</s>,
the sage named <s>Kaṇiṅka</s>, became skilled in policy.
When a wise man has met with calamity through the wickedness of time, through a fault of fate,
or through what destiny has assigned, he should conduct himself with intelligence in distress.
This alone is always the means to future attainment of good fortune:
that a wise man should protect the body, the instrument for attaining the three aims of life, in times of danger.
Long ago, when the time had been struck by drought for twelve years,
when waters had become mere remnants of tales and people had been wasted by famine,
when the continuity of <s>dharma</s> had perished and the surface of the earth was strewn with corpses,
all the sages, abandoning the fire-deities, their discipline lost,
wandered about, their conventions destroyed and the groves of their hermitages burned up.
Then <s>Viśvāmitra</s>, wandering, came to the dwelling of a dog-cooker.
It stank with the fat of slaughtered animals and was garlanded with dried meat and bones;
it was a hamlet where hardship was the rule, spread with dog skins.
Its pots were filled with blood, and it was crowded with the company of dogs;
it was cramped with hanging sinews and full of fragments of skeletons.
Even there, his belly emaciated by hunger, the sage begged for alms.

children.text: arthamāno 'pi sa yadā tato lobhena kiṃcana ||
children.translated_text: But when, though he begged, he obtained nothing at all because of their greed,

children.text: tadā kṛcchrāṃ daśāṃ yātaḥ papāta bhuvi mūrchitaḥ
children.translated_text: then, reduced to a wretched condition, he fell fainting on the ground.
He thought, 'Ah, terrible! This calamity has come upon me.
Or else I will steal a small piece of dog meat at night like a thief.
One who seeks to preserve life may take anything from anywhere when stability has collapsed on every side.
For in danger the preservation of life is the first sprout of <s>dharma</s>.'
While he was thinking this, the black night set in,
as if covered with the wings of countless crows cheated by the dog-cooker.

children.text: sa saktikāṃ snāyutantrīṃ lambamānāṃ vicintya saḥ ||
children.translated_text: Considering a sinew-stringed haunch that was hanging there,
he slowly reached the door of the hut and, trembling, set about taking it.
Inside, awake though pretending to sleep, his eyes clogged with phlegm,
an old man living by dogs spoke to him in a voice choked and rattling with cough:
'By whom is this sinew being pulled? I have not fallen under the power of sleep.

children.text: eṣa śastreṇa sahasā hanyate yo 'tra lambate
children.translated_text: Whoever is hanging about here will be killed at once with a weapon.'
Hearing this, <s>Viśvāmitra</s> said to him in a weak voice:
'I am <s>Kauśika</s>, a sage, reduced to thieving for the preservation of life.
Having obtained no alms and wasted by hunger, I am taking this dog's haunch.

children.text: adharmo nāturasyāsti ghoraṃ kṛcchraṃ gatasya ca
children.translated_text: There is no adharma for one who is afflicted and has fallen into terrible distress;

children.text: mūlaṃ ca jīvo dharmasya tasminnāpatsu rakṣyate ||
children.translated_text: and life is the root of <s>dharma</s>, so in danger it must be protected.
When it is protected, all the practices proper to good conduct begin again.'

children.text: ityukto muninā vṛddhaḥ samutthāya jagāda saḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus addressed by the sage, the old man rose up and said:
'Ah, lord, from greed for life you are praising sin.
You yourselves established the rule regarding what may and may not be eaten.
How, then, from fear of losing your life, do you turn toward sin?

children.text: na vārayāmi te māṃsaṃ vitarāmi na te svayam ||
children.translated_text: I am not preventing you from taking the meat, nor do I myself give it to you.
You are a teacher of all <s>dharma</s>s; do not, through delusion, go to hell.'
Hearing this from him, the sage spoke, stumbling again and again:

children.text: yasmiṃstapaśca satyaṃ ca svajñānaṃ ca pratiṣṭhitam
children.translated_text: 'In the body in which austerity, truth,
and one's own knowledge are established, when that body is protected, everything is protected.
Even after eating what must not be eaten, once released from danger to life,
Through merit gained in vows and at sacred fords, I shall wear away the sin.

children.text: ityuktvā tāṃ samādāya yayau tūrṇaṃ śvajāghanīm
children.translated_text: Having said this and taking up that dog’s haunch, he quickly went away.
At that very time clouds rained down abundance for the crops.
Thus, for the protection of life, even the sage formed a resolve regarding what was extremely condemned,
a resolve concerning dog’s meat; therefore one should protect life.
Hearing this, the son of <s>Dharma</s> asked <s>Bhīṣma</s> in amazement,
Grandfather, tell me the course of conduct for those who protect one who has sought refuge.
Asked this by the king, the son of <s>Śantanu</s> replied,
When questioned long ago by <s>Mucukunda</s>, <s>Bhārgava</s> told this story.
Long ago, in a forest, amid the great hardship of foul weather, a hunter,
contracted with cold, slept at night at the foot of a tree.
On the branch of that tree a pigeon had made his shelter,
and, remembering that his wife had not come even at day’s end, he grieved.
Tormented and distressed by separation from his beloved, he lamented;

children.text: kapotī tacca śuśrāva baddhā vyādhena pañjare ||
children.translated_text: the hen-pigeon heard that, though she had been bound by the hunter in a cage.

children.text: sā tamūce sukṛtino na prayānti viṣaṇṇatām
children.translated_text: She said to him, The virtuous do not sink into despondency;
this protection of one who has sought refuge is the foremost good deed.
The hunter is asleep here at the foot of the tree;

children.text: pūjāṃ vidhatsva śītārtaḥ śaraṇaṃ hyeṣa vāñchati ||
children.translated_text: honor him as is proper, for he is afflicted by cold and seeks refuge.
Hearing the words of his beloved, the bird said to the hunter,
Good sir, you have come to my house; I shall give you what you desire.
Hearing this, the hunter, afflicted by cold, asked him for fire,
and that bird too quickly brought fire down to him from above.
Then, when a fire well prepared with grass and leaves had been kindled,
the hunter, freed from cold but emaciated by hunger, asked him for food.
Eat me, the bird said out of compassion,
and himself entered the fire; seeing that, the hunter too fell into remorse.

children.text: sa tyaktvā kūṭayantrāṇi samutpāṭya ca pañjaram
children.translated_text: He abandoned his traps and devices and tore open the cage,
and, dispassionate, went into the forest, having undertaken a vow of fasting.
When the pigeon had gone to heaven in a celestial car bright as the sun,
the hen-pigeon, grieving for her husband, entered the fire.
When she was dwelling in the abode of the gods together with her husband,

children.text: dāvānale tanuṃ tyaktvā lubdhako 'pi divaṃ yayau ||
children.translated_text: the hunter too, abandoning his body in a forest fire, went to heaven.
How is sin, acquired by embodied beings through ignorance, destroyed?
Asked thus by <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, the son of <s>Śantanu</s> spoke again.
Long ago a king named <s>Pārikṣiti</s>, troubled by the killing of a brahmin,
went trustingly in the forest to the eminent sage named <s>Indota</s> for refuge.
Although repeatedly rejected by him, since he feared contact with sin,
the king, by compassionate words, brought him to a state of compassion.
As he recounted his sin, scorched by the fire of remorse,
and after he had bathed at sacred fords, that sage gradually became his officiating priest.
Then that king, his soul purified in due form by an <s>aśvamedha</s> sacrifice,
was delivered from terrible sin by compassionate <s>Indota</s>.

children.text: vyavasāyena buddhyā ca niścayena ca dehinaḥ
children.translated_text: By effort, by understanding, and by resolve, embodied beings cross beyond hell.
Long ago relatives were grieving over a child.
A vulture came to them and said, Go; abandon the child.

children.text: imāmavasthāṃ paryante ko nāma na gamiṣyati ||
children.translated_text: Who indeed, in the end, will not come to this condition?

children.text: mā tiṣṭhata ciraṃ ghore śmaśāne pretabāndhavāḥ
children.translated_text: Do not remain long in this dreadful cremation ground, kinsmen of the dead;
here thousands of mortals have gone, and will go, to destruction.
Hearing this, they abandoned the boy and slowly set out to go,
but a jackal came near and said, Shame on you, whose hearts are pitiless.

children.text: aho nu dāruṇā yūyaṃ tyaktvā gacchanti ye sutam
children.translated_text: Ah, how cruel you are, who abandon your son and go away!
Even those whose life-breaths are gone sometimes live again, their bodily elements merely asleep.

children.text: kiṃ vo bhayaṃ śmaśāne 'sminyāto 'staṃ na divākaraḥ
children.translated_text: What fear have you in this cremation ground? The sun has not yet set.
Even among animals a drop of compassion arises for this child.
When the jackal had spoken thus, the vulture, eater of corpses, again

children.text: gṛdhro jagāda citraṃ vo jambukasya girā bhramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: said to them, Strange indeed is your delusion through the jackal’s speech.
You possess the jewel of life; for one whose form is like wood or clod,

children.text: snehena pātajīvasya śiśoḥ kiṃ yāta mūḍhatām ||
children.translated_text: why, through affection for a child whose life has fallen away, do you go into folly?

children.text: vanaṃ vrajata vairāgyāttapaḥ kuruta vā mahat
children.translated_text: Go to the forest in detachment, or perform great austerity;
in <s>saṃsāra</s>, whose essence is separation, there is no refuge other than truth.

children.text: anyena vartmanā putraḥ pitā cānyena gacchati
children.translated_text: The son goes by one path, and the father by another;
in the other world beings go by their own deeds, so abandon the disturbance of attachment.
The old go, and the young, and children, and those still in the womb as well;

children.text: kriyate kiṃ vicāro 'sti na kālasya pramāthinaḥ ||
children.translated_text: what deliberation is there to make? There is no measure for destroying Time.
They declare that clear knowledge of the situation is this discharge of debt to kinsmen;

children.text: mṛtaḥ pralāpaṃ bāṣpaṃ ca na śṛṇoti na paśyati ||
children.translated_text: the dead man neither hears nor sees lamentation and tears.

children.text: vatsarāṇāṃ sahasraṃ me sāgraṃ jātasya vartate
children.translated_text: More than a thousand years have passed since my birth;
I have never seen one whose life has departed raised up by lamentations.
When the vulture had spoken thus and fallen silent, the jackal again said,
Show compassion to this lovely lotus-eyed child.
Before the killing of <s>Śambuka</s>, even the dead brahmin’s son
obtained the rare gift of life in the kingdom of <s>Rāma</s>, foe of the ten-necked one.
Perhaps the father, gone as a meritorious man to the next world,
will one day drink the handful of water offered by the two hands of this child.
When the jackal had spoken thus, the vulture again said to them,

children.text: santaḥ śokāmaye nṝṇāṃ na praśaṃsanti bheṣajam ||
children.translated_text: Good men do not praise medicine for people afflicted with the disease of grief.
At the end of the day this cremation ground becomes more terrible,
with circles of ghosts and vetālas adorned with garlands of skeletons.

children.text: kṣaṇena hi na gīryante sahasrāṇi bhavādṛśām
children.translated_text: For in a moment thousands like you are swallowed up.
Do not set your mind on this painful, disastrous quarrel.

children.text: vapuṣāṃ jīvitānāṃ ca gatānām āgamaḥ kutaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Whence is there any return of bodies and lives once they have gone?
Seeing the kinsmen turn back because of the vulture's words,
